t: Minimum Increase to Maximize Special Indices
o:
A special index strictly exceeds both neighbors. Only increases are allowed, and raising a non-special element never helps (it only raises the bar for adjacent candidates), so each potential special index i has an independent cost c[i] = max(0, max(nums[i-1], nums[i+1]) + 1 − nums[i]). Adjacent indices cannot both be special (each would need to exceed the other), so we select a maximum-cardinality set of pairwise non-adjacent interior indices minimizing total cost — a weighted independent-set DP done lexicographically (max count first, then min cost).

Example 1: cost[1] = max(1,2)+1−2 = 1 → answer 1. Example 2: cost[1] = 2, cost[2] = 3; best single special is index 1 → 2. Example 3: cost[1] = 4, cost[3] = 0; indices 1 and 3 are non-adjacent, both taken → 4.
k: Neighbors of a chosen special index are never worth raising, so costs are independent per candidate.
Adjacent indices cannot both be special, reducing the problem to a maximum-weight (lexicographic) independent set on a path — solvable with a simple linear DP.

a.n: Approach 1: Linear DP over indices with (count, cost) pairs
a.i: Let dp[i] = best (count, cost) considering indices 0..i. Either skip i (dp[i-1]) or make i special (dp[i-2] plus (1, c[i])), comparing pairs by count first then cost. Rolling two variables gives O(1) memory.
s: Sweep i from 0..n-1 maintaining dp[i-1] and dp[i-2].
Transition: dp[i] = better(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + (1, c[i])) with lexicographic comparison.
Return the cost component of dp[n-1].
a.t: O(n) — one pass with O(1) work per index

a.n: Approach 2: Explicit DP table (easier to trace)
a.i: Same recurrence but stored in full arrays dpCount[i] and dpCost[i], which makes reconstruction of the chosen indices straightforward — useful if a follow-up asks which operations to perform. Slightly more memory, identical time.
s: Fill dpCount/dpCost arrays bottom-up with the skip/take transition.
Optionally backtrack from dpCount[n-1] to recover the chosen special indices.

w: The rolling-variable version is the one to write under time pressure. Key pitfalls: computing costs against original neighbor values (neighbors are never raised), remembering the first and last indices can never be special, and using 64-bit costs (up to ~1e9 per index times 5e4 indices). Follow-up: reconstruct the actual set of operations, or allow decreases too (which breaks independence and needs a different model).
